judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Over-the-top panic ('airborne demons from the underworld', 'Nox's vital interests'), a flat functional captive ('Please take me back to the elevator.') and a mechanical journal with a count: Westwood throughout.

items.label: B
items.critique: Well-shaped and sentimental, with a second captive conveniently revealed and a precise location ('past the old ore chutes, on the east side'); the emotional coherence is tidier than Westwood's.

items.label: C
items.critique: Elevated diction ('Thieving, lumbering brutes!', 'abominable creatures', 'you will not find me ungrateful', 'Liberate my men') and a 'cold will finish what the Trolls began' flourish are a novelist's, not Nox's.

items.label: D
items.critique: The rescued pet frog and the 'Loads and loads of money?' gag are Westwood's dry slapstick; the captive's grumpy 'Fine! I will follow you!' seals it.

items.label: E
items.critique: Story-chaining exposition ('While you were running [Place], the express elevator jammed'), stilted 'We best go' and an over-chatty captive with a secret passage: authentic campaign connective tissue.

items.label: F
items.critique: Terse, crude stakes ('before the Ogres eat them'), 'my boy', 'damsels', and a thanks that immediately sends you to the next groups: Westwood's brisk, slightly dated tone.

items.label: G
items.critique: Laconic, characterful voice ('Worth your while. Deal?'), a talking crow and a wistful backstory for the reward robe; charming but modern indie-game minimalism, not Nox.

items.label: H
items.critique: Mannered priest ('I fear some abominable fate has befallen them', 'Let us make an arrangement, you and I') and a hint-giving reminder ('east of the ford'); same 'Liberate ... bring them home' formula as C.

items.label: I
items.critique: Run-on plea with missing comma, a captive speaking in exclamatory exposition and the 'menfolk cannot live without us' joke: Westwood's period humour.

items.label: J
items.critique: Whimsical comic old master ('He never misses his supper!', Imps that tickle, 'lost half my beard', 'I'm free!!!'): the gags are too cosy and written-up for Nox.

tells: New texts give every character a crafted personality and a distinct comic or sentimental bit (the crow's 'Rawk!', the beard, the reward's backstory); Westwood's captives speak in flat function lines ('I'll follow you.', 'Help us!').

New plea-givers use elevated or mannered diction ('Liberate', 'abominable', 'you will not find me ungrateful', 'Let us make an arrangement'); Westwood's speak plainly and loudly, with exclamation marks and run-ons.
New reminders add a precise location hint (the old well behind the smokehouse, east of the ford, the cellars); Westwood's reminders just urge haste or restate the reward.

Westwood's rescues link to the wider plot (the Captain is waiting, go find the other groups, the Chief Engineer) and carry blunt, dated humour; new ones are self-contained vignettes with tidy emotional closure.
New texts reuse a formula across quests ('Liberate ... and bring them home', 'take this ... as a token of my appreciation').
